title: Pediatric nondysraphic intramedullary spinal cord lipomas: surgical burden, reoperations, and long-term outcomes.
journal: Child's nervous system : ChNS : official journal of the International Society for Pediatric Neurosurgery
abstract: Spinal cord lipomas without spinal dysraphism are rare tumors but can cause substantial neurological deficits. Resection is particularly challenging owing to tight tumor-cord interface and there is no clear consensus regarding the management in the pediatric population. Therefore, we review our experience treating a cohort of pediatric patients with intramedullary lipomas. A database of pediatric patients surgically treated for intramedullary spinal cord tumors at a large comprehensive cancer center and affiliated children's hospital was reviewed between 2012 and 2025. Cases with a confirmed histology of lipoma were included. Demographic, surgical, and outcome data were collected. Seven patients were identified with spinal cord lipomas, with a median age of 9 years. All tumors spanned the cervical cord. Symptoms included pain, paresthesias, numbness, weakness, and bowel/bladder dysfunction. Five patients required repeat surgeries for hardware failure, repeat debulking, cerebrospinal fluid leak, and scoliosis repair. Two patients had long-term tumor progression. Surgical decision-making in pediatric intramedullary lipomas needs to balance maximal safe resection with the risk of iatrogenic deficits. Patients should be counseled about the significant risks and need for lifelong monitoring. In our series, reoperations were frequent and included both disease-related (repeat debulking/detethering) and treatment-related (CSF leak, deformity, and hardware complications). Early intervention before patients develop debilitating symptoms may help maximize long-term neurological outcomes.

title: Distinct prelimbic microcircuits control sensory and affective dimensions of neuropathic pain.
abstract: The microcircuit mechanisms underlying deactivation and altered output of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), a common feature of several chronic pain conditions, are poorly understood. Here, using unbiased in vivo longitudinal multiphoton imaging in the mouse prelimbic cortex (PrL), we show that nerve injury induces sensitization of all classes of GABAergic interneurons and a phenotypic switch from unimodal to polymodal responses. Through circuit interrogation, we identified functions for caudal geminal eminence-derived Prox1+ interneurons and revealed that distinct classes of inhibitory and excitatory neurons in the PrL have different functions in promoting neuropathic pain. In addition, we show that the sensory and affective dimensions of neuropathic pain engaged two distinct microcircuits, PV+-Rbp4+ neurons and Prox1+-Cux2+/Ntsr1+ neurons, respectively, to control distinct projection outputs. These findings provide a mechanistic basis for how mPFC guides actions to avoid or overcome pain and how prefrontal deactivation exacerbates neuropathic pain.

title: Cytokines in brain development.
abstract: Cytokines are central regulators of brain development and function, integrating genetic programs with maternal, immune and environmental signals. Although only a few cytokines have been examined in detail within the developing brain, existing evidence indicates that their effects are often profound and cytokine-specific. Here we review mechanistic studies in animal models that reveal how cytokines influence key neurodevelopmental processes, including progenitor cell-fate decisions, neuronal differentiation, synapse formation, synapse elimination and vascular integrity. Cytokines contribute to physiological circuit refinement and tissue maintenance, but they can also transmit peripheral immune signals to the brain, perturbing neurodevelopment and increasing susceptibility to subsequent behavioural and psychiatric disorders. We propose that rigorous and comprehensive mechanistic investigation of cytokine function during brain development will reveal therapeutic targets for neurodevelopmental disorders and immune-mediated neuropsychiatric diseases.

title: Automated retinal layer thickness segmentation in neovascular age-related macular degeneration: a comparison of two algorithms.
abstract: To evaluate the consistency of retinal measurements provided by two automated segmentation algorithms in eyes with neovascular age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Retrospective cohort study. Fifty patients with neovascular AMD. Retinal thickness was measured using a Heidelberg Spectralis HRA + OCT spectral-domain device. Measurements were automatically averaged across ETDRS grid subfields centered on the fovea using both the Spectralis built-in software (version 1.10.4.0) and the Orion automated OCT segmentation software (Voxeleron, version 3.0.0). Differences in quantitative retinal thickness metrics between the two algorithms. For inner retinal thickness, the mean difference was 8.97 μm in the central fovea (R² = 0.32), with larger variability in the inner (22.09-28.73 μm; R² = 0.32-0.80) and outer circles (16.02-29.50 μm; R² = 0.45-0.41). Outer retinal thickness showed smaller differences, with a mean of 21.51 μm in the central fovea (R² = 0.36) and modest variation across subfields. The neurosensory retina demonstrated a mean difference of 0.13 μm centrally (R² = 0.66), increasing across ETDRS subfields, with an overall mean difference of 45.30μm (R² = 0.82). Total retinal thickness differed by 43.54 μm centrally (R² = 0.61), with smaller differences across the grid (mean 18.16 μm; R² = 0.60). While correlations between the two segmentation algorithms were moderate to strong for several metrics, clinically meaningful mean differences were observed in specific compartments, most notably for central neurosensory and total retinal thickness. These findings indicate that the two algorithms should not be used interchangeably.

title: Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation - from gene discovery to therapeutic strategies.
abstract: Precision therapeutics are emerging for various neurological disorders, most notably single-gene disorders. Development of breakthrough treatments typically requires insight into the earliest pathogenic changes, which enables intervention before irreversible damage to cell function has occurred. At the extreme, presymptomatic gene therapy could subvert entire disease processes. The neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA) disorders exemplify progress from Mendelian disease gene discovery to the era of precision neurotherapeutics. These disorders highlight the opportunities and challenges in developing precision therapeutics for single-gene neurological disorders. In this Review, we discuss the most common NBIA disorders to highlight how the study of genetic disorders can provide insight into basic neuroscience and the brain's regional vulnerability. We discuss in detail the biology of pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN), which underscores the complex and poorly understood biochemistry of this apparently simple inborn error of vitamin metabolism, and also forges a path for novel interventions. The progress in understanding of and therapeutic development for PKAN exemplifies the beginning of a rise in breakthrough therapies for genetic neurological disorders.

title: A systematic review and meta-analysis exploring the effects of tDCS on metabolic syndrome parameters in adults.
abstract: Metabolic syndrome is a group of health conditions associated with obesity, increased risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and mortality. Interventions, including lifestyle changes, pharmacological treatments, and surgical interventions, have limited long-term efficacy, and do not adequately address some underpinning factors in overweight/obesity, such as cognitive/inhibitory control related to eating behaviours. There is emerging evidence for the successful use of neuromodulation techniques, such as transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), as potential adjunctive therapies for eating and weight disorders. This systematic review and meta-analysis have investigated the potential effects of tDCS on weight and metabolic parameters, in adults with or without excess body weight. In accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement, a systematic search of Embase, PsychInfo and PubMed electronic databases was performed to identify randomised clinical trials (RCTs) of tDCS which reported at least one metabolic syndrome parameter. Primary outcomes were weight, body mass index (BMI), waist circumference, blood pressure, blood glucose, insulin, and lipid profile. A total of 28 studies (1129 participants) were included. tDCS protocols varied in stimulation sites, current intensity, and number and duration of sessions. Meta-analyses showed small but statistically significant weight loss (MD = -1.16 kg, 95% CI: -2.29 to -0.02; p = 0.04) and waist circumference reduction (MD = -0.67 cm, 95% CI: -1.14 to -0.19; p = 0.02) following active tDCS compared to sham. A non-significant reduction in food cravings traits was observed (SMD = -0.21, p = 0.06). Effects on glucose and blood pressure were variable. The modest positive effects of tDCS on weight and waist circumference, nonetheless, highlight its potential clinical relevance for treating obesity and metabolic syndrome. Well-powered RCTs using standardised assessment procedures are essential to clarify the therapeutic mechanisms of tDCS and to identify optimal dosing for this population.

title: Principles and assumptions underlying domain detection in spatial transcriptomics.
abstract: Spatial-omics technologies simultaneously measure feature expression and locations within tissues, providing an unprecedented opportunity to study tissue structures. The first key step in analyzing these high-dimensional datasets is identifying biologically relevant clusters, yet the large number of spatial-omics clustering (SOC) methods makes method selection challenging. Here we comprehensively review 47 SOC methods and extract information on 108 variables across 26 groups of method characteristics and applicability. This revealed substantial diversity in the underlying algorithms, affecting the suitability of methods to different tissues and biotechnologies. Based on this, we provide an analytical decision tree to help data analysts select methods based on their data types and research questions, and we highlight knowledge gaps to help bioinformaticians identify new avenues for method development. We thus hope to pave the way for more effective applications in a diverse methodological landscape and guide future method development.

title: Risk of falls and delirium associated with dual orexin receptor antagonists versus benzodiazepines and Z-drugs in older adults with dementia.
abstract: Insomnia in older adults with dementia is commonly treated with benzodiazepines (BZDs) and Z drugs, despite safety concerns. Evidence on dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORAs) in this population remains limited. Therefore, this study aimed to compare safety outcomes of DORAs versus BZDs/Z drugs in older adults with dementia and insomnia. This retrospective observational cohort study used electronic health records from TriNetX Global Collaborative Network. From 17,226 eligible adults aged ≥65 years with dementia and insomnia, 734 matched pairs were included after propensity score matching. Participants received DORAs (suvorexant, lemborexant, or daridorexant) or BZDs/Z drugs within 1 month of dementia diagnosis. Primary outcomes were falls and delirium over 12 months. Secondary outcomes included hospitalization, mortality, and emergency department visits. Among 734 matched pairs (mean age 83.5 years; 65-66% female), DORA use was associated with significantly lower risk of falls (HR 0.35, 95% CI 0.18-0.71; P = 0.003), delirium (HR 0.39, 95% CI 0.23-0.65; P < 0.001), hospitalization (HR 0.31, 95% CI 0.21-0.47; P < 0.001), and emergency department visits (HR 0.32, 95% CI 0.20-0.50; P < 0.001). No significant difference in mortality was observed (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.53-1.11; P = 0.154). In conclusion, DORA was associated with substantially lower risks of falls, delirium, hospitalization, and emergency visits compared with BZDs/Z drugs in older adults with dementia. DORAs may offer a safer alternative to BZDs/Z drugs for managing insomnia in older adults with dementia, potentially reducing fall-related injuries and healthcare utilization.

title: APOE ε4 carriership status enhances age-related changes in Alzheimer's disease plasma biomarkers concentrations.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) plasma biomarkers are cost-effective tools to detect early stage amyloid pathology. We investigated how interactions between AD genetic risk (apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4, AD polygenic risk score (excluding APOE; PRSAD)), age, and sex affected AD plasma biomarkers concentrations in a population-based cohort. We included 5913 participants from the Netherlands Twin Register age 30 - 80 (64.1% females, 29.8% ε4 carriers) and measured plasma phosphorylated-tau-217 (p-tau217), amyloid-β-42/40 (Aβ-42/40), neurofilament light (NfL), and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). We showed that the PRSAD did not associate with biomarker concentrations over age. In ε4 carriers, decreases in Aβ-42/40 became steeper after age 50, and increases in p-tau217 and GFAP became steeper after age 55 and 60 compared to non-carriers, respectively. Analyses in a separate longitudinal cohort (EMIF-AD) confirmed that p-tau217 concentration changes in ε4 carriers reflect AD pathology. These results highlight the potential of plasma biomarkers, especially p-tau217, for early detection of preclinical AD pathology.

title: Autism-relevant oxysterol signaling regulates GABAergic neurogenesis and interneuron subtype specification.
abstract: Disturbances in GABAergic neurodevelopment are thought to underlie cortical network dysfunction in neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) such as autism and schizophrenia. The diversity of GABAergic neurons is shaped by cortical cues during prolonged postmitotic differentiation, yet how pathological environments associated with NDDs influence this process remains poorly understood. Oxysterols, oxidized cholesterol metabolites or its precursors, modulate key developmental signaling pathways. Here, using an iPSC-based model of human forebrain GABAergic neuron differentiation combined with single-cell transcriptomics, we show that 24S,25-epoxycholesterol, an oxysterol enriched in the fetal brain and dysregulated in NDDs, enhances neurogenesis while altering the distribution of GABAergic neuronal subtypes. Pharmacological and genetic perturbations further identify the liver X receptor as a critical mediator of these effects. Together, these findings uncover a link between cholesterol metabolism and GABAergic fate specification, suggesting that aberrant oxysterol signaling contributes to the pathogenesis of NDDs.

title: Frequency-specific structure-function decoupling underlies core symptoms in schizophrenia.
abstract: A major challenge in schizophrenia is its clinical heterogeneity, which has obstructed biomarker identification. Recent research indicates that frequency-specific structural eigenmodes, which govern distinct spatiotemporal propagation patterns, are linked to the functions of unimodal and transmodal regions. Notably, differential dysfunction in these regions has previously been associated with specific symptoms of schizophrenia. Based on this, we hypothesized that frequency-specific SC-FC decoupling underlies the core symptoms in schizophrenia. To test this hypothesis, our study examined 42 patients with schizophrenia versus 51 healthy controls. Low- and high-frequency components were extracted from structural connectivity and fed into a deep attention network to predict functional connectivity. Frequency-specific coupling values were computed to assess their associations with clinical symptom scores. Additionally, relationships between coupling differences and neurotransmitter distributions as well as gene expression profiles were examined. Our results showed that patients exhibited frequency-specific SC-FC decoupling. Low-frequency coupling between the default mode and sensorimotor networks correlated with hallucination severity, while intra-sensorimotor low-frequency coupling was associated with delusions and insufficient spontaneity and conversational fluidity; high-frequency intra-sensorimotor coupling was also linked to conversational deficits. Between-group coupling differences were significantly associated with specific neurotransmitter distributions and gene expression patterns. Taken together, these findings demonstrate that frequency-specific SC-FC decoupling may underlie the core symptoms of schizophrenia, providing mechanistic insight and a potential foundation for precision-targeted interventions.

title: Nectin3 on prefrontal excitatory and inhibitory neurons distinctly mediates adolescent stress-induced cognitive and social deficits.
abstract: Adolescence represents a critical period for prefrontal circuit maturation and heightened vulnerability to stress-related psychopathology. Chronic social defeat stress (CSDS) during adolescence is known to induce enduring cognitive and social deficits, yet the prefrontal molecular mechanisms that mediate these impairments remain poorly understood. Here, we identify the synaptic adhesion molecule nectin3 as a key modulator of adolescent CSDS-induced behavioral dysfunction through cell-type-specific actions in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) of adolescent mice. We first demonstrate that CSDS downregulates nectin3 expression in both excitatory and inhibitory neurons in the mouse mPFC. Genetic knockdown and overexpression manipulations of mPFC nectin3 establish its causal involvement. Crucially, cell-type-specific interventions reveal a double dissociation: nectin3 in excitatory neurons selectively mediates cognitive deficits in temporal order memory and spatial working memory, while nectin3 in inhibitory neurons preferentially regulates social behavior. Structural and electrophysiological measures further revealed that nectin3 knockdown in excitatory (not inhibitory) neurons leads to spine loss and reduced frequency of the miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents in pyramidal neurons, potentially linking nectin3 reduction with cognitive deficits induced by CSDS. These findings reveal cell-specific nectin3 functions underlying different domains of behavioral alterations following adolescent stress, which may serve as potential intervention targets for developing symptom-specific therapeutic strategies against stress-related psychiatric disorders.

title: Novel Mn(II) Quinaldinate Complexes With Halogenated Imidazo[1,2-a]pyridine and Memantine: Synthesis, Spectroscopic Studies, and Selective Pro-Apoptotic and Pro-Oxidative Activity in Cancer Cells.
abstract: Three novel Mn(II) complexes incorporating quinaldinate and biologically relevant N-donor ligands-halogenated imidazo[1,2-a]pyridine derivatives-were synthesized and comprehensively characterized in the solid state by single-crystal X-ray diffraction, FT-IR, Raman spectroscopy, and thermal analysis. The investigated compounds include two unprecedented one-dimensional coordination polymers, [Mn2(6-Brimpy)2(QA)4]n (1) and [Mn2(6-Climpy)2(QA)4]n (2), and the mononuclear complex [Mn(QA)3](H2O)⋅(mem) (3). FT-IR studies in DMSO suggested the persistence of coordination species derived from compounds 1-3, while allowing for changes in solution speciation. UV-vis and emission measurements revealed ligand-centered absorption and pronounced luminescence, indicating that the obtained systems combine selective biological activity with promising photophysical properties. Biological evaluation against metastatic melanoma (1205-Lu), glioblastoma (T98G), and normal dermal fibroblasts (NHDF) demonstrated moderate but selective anticancer activity, with the strongest effect observed for complex 2 toward 1205-Lu cells, while all compounds remained essentially nontoxic toward NHDF fibroblasts. Mechanistic studies revealed a concentration-dependent increase in caspase-3 activity and malondialdehyde levels in melanoma cells, indicating apoptosis induction accompanied by oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation. Importantly, the free ligands alone did not exhibit significant anticancer activity, demonstrating that coordination to Mn(II) is essential for the emergence and enhancement of the observed biological effects.

title: [Mechanism of acupuncture at governor vessel acupoints in improving cognitive dysfunction in AD mice based on complement C1q-mediated microglial synaptic phagocytosis].
journal: Zhongguo zhen jiu = Chinese acupuncture & moxibustion
abstract: To explore the possible mechanism of acupuncture at governor vessel (GV) acupoints in improving cognitive dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease (AD) mice based on complement C1q-mediated aberrant activation of microglia and excessive synaptic phagocytosis. Twenty male APP/PS1 double transgenic mice were randomly divided into a model group and an acupuncture group, with 10 mice in each group; ten male C57BL/6 mice were selected as the control group. In the acupuncture group, acupuncture was applied at "Baihui" (GV20), "Dazhui" (GV14) and "Mingmen" (GV4), 20 min each time, once daily, 5 times a week for 4 consecutive weeks. The learning-memory ability of mice was assessed by Morris water maze test, the synaptic ultrastructure in hippocampal CA1 region was observed by transmission electron microscope, the positive expression of postsynaptic density protein 95 (PSD-95) and ionized calcium-binding adapter molecule 1 (IBA-1) in hippocampal tissue was detected by immunofluorescence, the protein expression of IBA-1, complement C1q and SMAD-specific E3 ubiquitin protein ligase 1 (SMURF1) in hippocampal tissue was detected by Western blot, the ubiquitination modification of C1q protein was predicted by UbiBrowser and further verified by co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP). Compared with the control group, in the model group, the escape latency was prolonged (P<0.01), the number of platform crossings was reduced (P<0.01); decreased number of synapses, damaged synaptic structure, and thinner and looser postsynaptic density could be observed in the hippocampal CA1 region; the positive expression of IBA-1 and the protein expression of C1q and IBA-1 were increased (P<0.01), the positive expression of PSD-95 and the protein expression of SMURF1 were decreased (P<0.01) in hippocampal tissue. Compared with the model group, in the acupuncture group, the escape latency was shortened (P<0.05), the number of platform crossings was increased (P<0.05); increased number of synapses, improved synaptic structure, and thicker and denser postsynaptic density could be observed in hippocampal CA1 region; the positive expression of IBA-1 and the protein expression of C1q and IBA-1 were decreased (P<0.01, P<0.05), the positive expression of PSD-95 and the protein expression of SMURF1 were increased (P<0.01, P<0.05) in hippocampal tissue. SMURF1 was identified as the E3 ligase for C1q protein, and SMURF1 could bind to C1q. Acupuncture at GV acupoints directly or indirectly reduces C1q level in the hippocampus, inhibits the classical complement system and excessive microglial activation, reduces aberrant synaptic phagocytosis, and thereby improves cognitive dysfunction in AD mice.

Advancing the Alzheimer's disease research and care pipeline with agentic artificial intelligence: Opportunities, challenges, and priorities from the international clinical trials on Alzheimer's disease (CTAD) task force.
journal: The journal of prevention of Alzheimer's disease
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) holds unprecedented potential to transform the entire Alzheimer's Disease and related dementias (ADRD) research and care continuum. During the 2025 Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease (CTAD) conference, the CTAD Task Force reviewed recent advances in the field, highlighting the emerging role of agentic AI, and discussed priorities to guide future AI-driven innovation in ADRD. Agentic AI co-scientists are emerging as transformative tools to accelerate scientific discovery by autonomously integrating multimodal data, generating and evaluating new hypotheses, and connecting previously siloed knowledge into actionable insights. Operationalized through end-to-end translational pipelines, such platforms can also link mechanistic insights to therapeutic design by automating molecular docking and drug repurposing. Complementary initiatives are creating digital wet labs for in silico experimentation. At the same time, agentic AI is increasingly being used to address pre-discovery bottlenecks by automating data harmonization and inferring missing information through digital twins and synthetic data. AI is also reshaping next-generation ADRD clinical trials, through automated assessment of clinical outcomes, precision participant stratification, individualized disease trajectory modeling and prediction of treatment response. These approaches could substantially improve trial efficiency through responder enrichment. Importantly, AI applications are expanding beyond discovery and clinical trials to support diagnosis, care navigation, and personalized disease management. To translate the momentum surrounding AI innovation into meaningful and sustainable impact across the ADRD continuum, the Task Force identified priorities including the development of AI-ready ecosystems, closer collaboration between clinicians, researchers and computer scientists, AI-enabled optimization of clinical trials and robust ethical and governance frameworks for responsible AI adoption.

Selective and spatially biased activity remodeling following adult-onset sensory loss.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Cross-modal brain plasticity after sensory loss allows an organism to utilize the remaining senses to guide behavior. Two distinct mechanisms support such adaptation: cross-modal recruitment and compensatory plasticity. Cross-modal recruitment refers to the deprived sensory areas gaining responsiveness to the spared senses, while compensatory plasticity indicates enhanced functionality of the spared sensory areas. Widespread synaptic and circuit-level plasticity has been reported to support such cross-modal plasticity. Here we combined whole-brain clearing, light-sheet imaging, and activity labeling using a cFosTRAP2 mouse line to examine the spatial distribution of highly active cells across brain areas following acute sensory manipulations in adult mice of both sexes. Adult-onset vision loss led to an initial decrease in the density of activity-labeled cells in visual areas, including the primary visual cortex (V1), and a parallel increase in the spared primary auditory (A1) and somatosensory barrel (S1BF) cortices. V1 and some higher-order visual areas (HVAs), but not the visual thalamus, exhibited a partial rebound in activity after a week of vision loss. The activity rebound in visual cortices and the enhanced activity observed in A1 were spatially biased. Passively exposing adult-onset blind mice to sound did not further alter activity levels, except for a decrease in the claustrum. Conversely, adult-onset deafening significantly reduced the activity-labeled cell density in auditory and auditory-related areas without clear signs of compensatory plasticity in the spared areas. Our results indicate that adult cross-modal plasticity is largely observed in sensory cortices with rather specific within-area spatial bias, suggesting selective functional adaptations.Significance Statement This study examined the spatial profile of how the adult brain adapts when one sense is lost. In mice, vision loss caused brain activity to drop in visual areas followed by partial recovery over time, suggesting gradual recruitment of these areas by non-visual information. In parallel, the brain areas for hearing and touch became more active, a sign of compensation. Activity changes were not widespread but limited mainly to sensory areas with some local spatial bias. In contrast, the same duration of hearing loss produced much less evidence of compensation in the spared sensory areas. These findings suggest that the adult brain can reorganize after sensory loss, but this adaptation is selective and region-specific, implying targeted functional compensation.

title: RAI1 loss produces cell type-specific transcriptomic, circuit, and behavioural consequences across mPFC GABAergic interneuron subtypes.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Haploinsufficiency of RAI1 (retinoic acid-induced 1) causes Smith-Magenis syndrome (SMS), a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by intellectual disability, maladaptive behaviours, and social deficits. RAI1 is a transcriptional regulator broadly expressed across multiple brain cell types, yet the cell type-specific transcriptional consequences of Rai1 haploinsufficiency remain unknown. Behavioural experiments used mice of both sexes. Our spatial transcriptomic assays in Rai1 +/- mice identified dysregulated genes across isocortical cell types, with synaptic organization and activity-dependent programs affected in a subtype-specific manner among GABAergic interneurons. To explore RAI1 function in these cells, we conditionally deleted Rai1 from parvalbumin (PV), somatostatin (SST), and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) interneurons. In the social dominance tube test, PV- and SST-specific Rai1 loss reduced winning rates, whereas VIP-specific loss increased winning. Rai1 ⁺/⁻ mice showed social competition-induced PV/VIP cFos activation in the medial-prefrontal cortex. Overall mPFC cFos activity was increased in VIP mutants but was decreased in PV and SST mutants. Monosynaptic rabies tracing revealed RAI1-dependent, subtype-specific remodeling of long-range inputs onto mPFC interneurons. Chemogenetic inhibition of Rai1-deficient mPFC PV or VIP interneurons normalized the social competition phenotypes. Together, our findings reveal that Rai1 haploinsufficiency induces cell-type-specific transcriptional and anatomical reorganization of prefrontal interneurons, which bidirectionally biases social behaviour output and is acutely reversible by targeted activity modulation. By resolving how a broadly expressed gene produces divergent consequences across interneuron classes, our work clarifies the cellular origins of social deficits in SMS and points to subtype-selective interneuron modulation as a therapeutic strategy i SMS and GABAergic disorders.Significance statement Social behavioural deficits are a prominent feature of SMS, a neurodevelopmental disorder caused by haploinsufficiency of the transcriptional regulator RAI1 GABAergic interneuron subtypes in the medial prefrontal cortex are critical for social behaviour, but the transcriptional programs governing their functional development and maturation are largely unknown. Here we show that Rai1 loss causes subtype-specific transcriptomic and anatomical input reorganization, and altered Fos activity in PV, SST, and VIP interneurons, culminating in divergent social competitive outcomes. The net social deficit likely arises from competing cell-type-specific perturbations. Notably, acute modulation of interneuron activity normalizes social behaviour, highlighting a potential therapeutic opportunity. Our findings emphasize the need for subtype-specific interventions and provide a cell-type-resolved framework for understanding GABAergic dysfunction in neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: A dorsoventral gradient of synaptic dynamics across columns of the midbrain periaqueductal gray.
abstract: The midbrain periaqueductal gray (PAG) is an evolutionarily conserved, highly interconnected brain region that coordinates diverse physiological and behavioral responses essential for survival, including pain modulation, autonomic and cardiovascular regulation, and defensive responses to threat. The PAG is anatomically and functionally subdivided into longitudinal columns that generate divergent behavioral and physiological responses. However, little is known about how distinct synaptic properties of neurons in each column support column-specific information processing. To address this gap, we made whole-cell voltage-clamp recordings from unlabeled neurons in the ventrolateral (vl), lateral (l), and dorsomedial (dm) columns of PAG in adult male and female C57BL/6J mice. Our results demonstrate that many features of synaptic processing are conserved across columns, including the relative balance of synaptic inhibition/excitation as well as stable paired pulse ratios across a wide range of interstimulus intervals. Despite these commonalities, high frequency stimulation revealed significant cross-column differences in synaptic integration mechanisms. Specifically, phasic EPSC amplitudes remained stable in the vlPAG and, to a lesser extent, the lPAG. In stark contrast, high frequency stimulation resulted in pronounced temporal summation in the dmPAG, due to, in part, slower EPSC kinetics. This profile resulted in the generation of an envelope/slow current during high-frequency trains which counteracted more pronounced phasic EPSC depression observed in the dmPAG. Together, these results identify column-specific strategies to preserve excitatory signal transfer across the PAG, providing a synaptic basis for how distinct columns process information to support their specialized functional roles.eNeuro Assessment The study investigates synaptic properties of periaqueductal grey (PAG) neurons in distinct divisions. The authors report convincing data for division-specific synaptic dynamics. The experiments are rigorously designed, the data are of high quality, and the statistical power and analyses are appropriate. The results provide important information about region-specific response properties within the PAG and have implication for the interpretation of the contribution of this circuit to behavior.

title: Coincidence detection in aspiny interneuron dendrites.
abstract: Recent evidence for long-term potentiation (LTP) at glutamatergic synapses on GABAergic interneurons calls for close attention to the sub-cellular phenomena that underlie the induction of plasticity in aspiny dendrites. Neurogliaform interneurons exhibit large NMDA receptor-mediated currents, Hebbian LTP and supralinear summation of glutamatergic signals converging on dendritic compartments. Dendritic supralinearity in interneurons does not require sodium channels. Here we investigate the principles governing supralinear synaptic integration and its interaction with backpropagating action potentials in the synaptic plasticity context. We developed a biophysically realistic, multi-compartmental model of a murine (Mus musculus, male and female) hippocampal neurogliaform interneuron, with dendritic architecture and ion channel densities tuned to match ex vivo recordings. The interaction between synaptic inputs and action potentials was tested with patch-clamp electrophysiology and two-photon imaging of dendritic calcium-dependent fluorescence transients. Whether simulated glutamatergic excitatory postsynaptic potentials are clustered on a dendritic fragment or dispersed across the entire arbor, they summate supralinearly as assessed from the calculated somatic voltage response. Clustered inputs induce more pronounced local depolarizations and calcium transients than dispersed inputs. Action potentials generated at the soma backpropagate throughout the dendritic arbor but are attenuated at branch points. Coincident synaptic input and backpropagating action potentials relieve this attenuation, further enhance dendritic depolarizations, and greatly potentiate calcium influx via NMDA receptors. Despite differences in dendritic anatomy and in the roles of sodium channels, the interplay of orthodromic and antidromic voltage propagation and resultant calcium signal amplification exhibits remarkable similarities between neurogliaform interneurons and principal cells.Significance Statement Neurogliaform interneurons are key regulators of brain circuit activity, yet the dendritic mechanisms that enable these inhibitory cells to undergo synaptic plasticity remain poorly understood. Combining biophysically realistic computer modeling with electrophysiology and two-photon calcium imaging, we show that coincident synaptic input and backpropagating action potentials strongly amplify dendritic depolarization and calcium influx in these interneurons. Although their dendrites lack spines and do not rely on sodium-channel-dependent dendritic spikes, neurogliaform interneurons nonetheless use computational principles remarkably similar to those of excitatory principal neurons. These findings advance the understanding of how inhibitory circuits support learning-related plasticity and may provide foundational insight into disorders such as epilepsy and schizophrenia, in which abnormal dendritic signalling and inhibitory dysfunction are implicated.

Speech and Language Abnormalities in Putative Brain-First Versus Body-First Parkinson's Disease.
journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
abstract: The α-synuclein origin model proposes brain-first and body-first Parkinson's disease (PD) subtypes, with speech potentially revealing their distinct neurodegenerative patterns. We aimed to analyze the possible speech and language differences between untreated PD patients with premotor (putative body-first) and without (putative brain-first) rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder. Speech samples of reading passages and monologues were automatically analyzed using acoustic and linguistic features. We enrolled 23 body-first and 35 brain-first de novo PD patients compared with 35 healthy controls. Brain-first patients showed greater speech impairment severity compared with body-first patients (P = 0.002) and controls (P < 0.001), whereas body-first patients showed greater language impairment severity compared with brain-first patients (P < 0.001) and controls (P < 0.001). Putative brain-first subtype had more motor speech abnormalities whereas body-first subtype manifested greater language impairment. Thes finding is consistent with motor-dominant nigrostriatal involvement in brain-first and broader non-motor/cognitive involvement in body-first PD. © 2026 The Author(s). title: The Role of Medical Therapy in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: An Updated Review.
abstract: This review highlights recent advances in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) treatment, focusing on how to effectively implement both traditional and novel pharmacologic strategies in clinical practice. Traditional medications like beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers continue to play a critical role. However, new treatments, such as cardiac myosin inhibitors, provide an innovative approach for relieving symptoms, especially in obstructive HCM cases. Emerging therapies, including sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors, sacubitril/valsartan, and ninerafaxstat, show promising benefits. Proper management of related conditions such as atrial fibrillation and heart failure is also essential. A comprehensive approach that considers individual patient characteristics and the specific subtype of HCM is essential for achieving optimal outcomes.

title: Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation for depression: From stress to adaptive brain recovery.
abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is among the most prevalent and disabling psychiatric disorders worldwide and remains associated with substantial unmet clinical need despite the availability of effective pharmacological, psychological, lifestyle, and neuromodulatory interventions. Psychoeducation is an important component of care for mood disorders because it can improve illness understanding, treatment engagement, adherence, self-management, and relapse prevention. However, conventional psychoeducation has not always incorporated advances in contemporary neuroscience. Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) extends traditional approaches by translating findings from affective neuroscience, stress biology, neuroplasticity, and brain-circuit research into accessible and clinically meaningful explanations for patients and families. By helping individuals understand depressive symptoms and treatment effects within a framework of adaptive brain recovery, NIPE may reduce self-blame and self-stigma, strengthen agency and treatment engagement, and support sustained recovery. This chapter reviews the epidemiology, clinical heterogeneity, and course of MDD; outlines key neurobiological mechanisms associated with depressive symptoms; and integrates evidence from psychoeducation with contemporary neuroscientific models. It also considers the application of NIPE across pharmacological, psychological, lifestyle, digital, and neuromodulatory interventions, together with the mechanisms through which NIPE may influence clinical outcomes. NIPE is proposed as a promising bridge between neuroscience, shared understanding, and personalised psychiatric care.

title: Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation for substance use disorder treatment: From brain awareness to brain recovery capital.
abstract: Substance use disorders continue to affect millions of people worldwide, yet a striking proportion never receive treatment. Poor awareness, internalized stigma, and neurobiological changes in the circuits responsible for self-monitoring all contribute to this gap in ways that conventional psychoeducation has not adequately addressed. Recent advances in addiction neuroscience offer a more precise and less stigmatizing language for understanding these barriers, one that reframes addiction as a brain disorder rather than a moral failure and opens new possibilities for how we educate patients about their condition. Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation, or NIPE, builds on this foundation. It integrates current addiction neuroscience into an educational program designed to improve insight, reduce shame, and strengthen motivation for treatment and recovery. This paper proposes a clinical stage-based NIPE framework organized around the Transtheoretical Model of Health Behavior Change, mapping specific educational content and delivery priorities to seven stages of the recovery trajectory. The goal is an approach that meets people where they actually are in both their motivational readiness and their neurobiological capacity to engage. An example of a NIPE package for recovery and future directions to deliver effective NIPE and promote brain recovery are discussed.

title: Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation for schizophrenia.
abstract: Schizophrenia remains a major challenge in psychiatric practice, characterized by a heterogenous constellation of symptoms, including positive symptoms (e.g., hallucinations and delusions), negative symptoms (e.g., social withdrawal and diminished motivation), cognitive impairments, and frequently, lack of insight. Standard psychoeducation has served as a vital partner to psychological medicine for decades, trying to reduce the relapse rates by emphasizing medication adherence. However, many conventional models often rely on descriptive clinical phenomenology that fails to resonate with the patient's subjective experience and rarely explain the neurological causes behind the hallucinations or illogical thinking. This disconnection can inadvertently reinforce stigma and fail to support the patient's remaining cognitive capacities to reinforce recovery. Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation (NIPE) emerges as a transformative paradigm, integrating cutting-edge insights from brain science into the educational dialogue. By establishing the explanation of symptoms in neurobiology and shifting the narrative from "mental illness" to "circuit dysfunction", NIPE aims to bypass psychological defenses, objectify the disorder, and foster a collaborative therapeutic alliance. This chapter presents the neurocognitive aspects of the psychoeducational content, the neurocognitive considerations that must be addressed when providing psychoeducation, and examples of NIPE for Schizophrenia, aiming to advance brain health literacy for practitioners who will support patients as active partners in recovery alongside daily functional restoration.

title: Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation for posttraumatic stress disorder.
abstract: Over the past several decades, substantial progress has been made in elucidating the neurobiological mechanisms underlying trauma exposure and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), including alterations in large-scale brain networks involved in threat detection, emotional regulation, and cognitive control. Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) represents a compelling approach for translating neuroscientific research to impact real-world clinical care. In this Chapter, we first summarize current neurobiological models of PTSD and the growing literature supporting how evidence-based treatments for PTSD, such as prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy, or medication-based approaches, at least partially target these neurobiological mechanisms thought to be maintaining symptoms. Next, we review the variable use of NIPE within evidence-based psychotherapies, including first-line treatments such as prolonged exposure (PE) and cognitive processing therapy (CPT) as well as second-line and emerging treatments. We also discuss the availability and limitations of stand-alone NIPE materials relevant to PTSD for clinicians, patients, and the public. Finally, we emphasize considerations and future directions for the field. This includes the need for (a) development of standardized, evidence-based NIPE materials that are grounded in sound neuroscientific evidence, emphasize neuroplasticity, are available in accessible and engaging formats, and are adaptable to diverse populations and contexts and (b) randomized controlled trials comparing NIPE materials to standard psychoeducation approaches. NIPE holds considerable potential to enhance treatment outcomes and reshape public understanding of trauma-related disorders, with its continued evolution requiring further research and development to fully realize these benefits.

title: Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation for OCD.
abstract: Obsessive-compulsive disorder is a relatively common psychiatric disorder that is associated with major impairment and suffering. Integration of how neurocircuitry is involved in the pathophysiology of OCD can provide further understanding and support of OCD as a 'brain-based disorder.' This chapter will discuss how to effectively diagnose OCD, including information about prevalence, subtypes, and risk factors. In addition, we will provide an overview of traditional psychological models of OCD as well as newer models that focus on multiple integrating circuits. The overarching focus of the chapter will be how to integrate neuroscience into education for patients with OCD as they move through the continuum of care, ranging from diagnosis to behavioral, pharmacological, and invasive and noninvasive direct circuit interventions.

title: Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation for bipolar disorder.
abstract: Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) extends traditional psychoeducation for bipolar disorder by grounding clinical content in the neural mechanisms underlying the illness. This chapter reviews the neuroscience foundation relevant to bipolar disorder, including prefrontal-limbic circuit dysfunction, reward processing abnormalities that shift between mood states, circadian rhythm disruption, autonomic dysregulation, and the neuroplastic changes linked to illness progression and recovery. We translate these mechanisms into accessible psychoeducational content addressing diagnosis, pathogenesis, risk factors, and treatment, and describe brain-based strategies spanning cognitive monitoring, circadian-focused interventions, and emerging digital phenotyping tools. Delivery considerations are addressed with attention to the state-dependent nature of insight and cognitive function across mood episodes, phenotype-specific personalization, and family involvement. We outline mechanisms through which NIPE may improve outcomes, including enhanced awareness, reduced stigma, improved treatment adherence, and greater self-efficacy. While empirical evaluation of NIPE specifically for bipolar disorder remains limited, the chapter identifies priorities for future research, including randomized trials, mechanistic mediation analyses, and precision medicine approaches tailored to bipolar phenotype and illness course.

title: Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation for anxiety: Translating brain-behavior models into scalable clinical tools.
abstract: Advances in affective and systems neuroscience have clarified how distributed brain networks encode threat processing, generate bodily arousal, and shape cognitive and behavioral features of anxiety disorders. However, this progress has not been systematically translated into patient-facing educational tools or clinical care. Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation (NIPE) extends conventional psychoeducation by incorporating brain-based explanations of symptoms and treatment, while also structuring materials to engage attention, memory, and self-referential processing. Emerging work suggests NIPE may enhance insight, reduce stigma, and improve treatment engagement and adherence. NIPE aims to optimize both the content (what is taught) and structure (how it is delivered) of psychoeducation to engage emotional and motivational aspects of learning. Building on recent NIPE frameworks applied to other psychiatric conditions (e.g., addiction), here we extend this approach to anxiety disorders. We developed two cartoon-based NIPE posters within an anxiety disorders specialty clinic to operationalize core brain-behavior processes in anxiety. The first poster (10 Ways Anxiety Impacts Your Health) organizes anxiety symptoms into four domains: threat-related Alarms, maladaptive Beliefs, reinforcing Coping Behaviors, and broader Social Context. The second poster (10 Actionable To Do's) maps evidence-based cognitive-behavioral strategies onto corresponding brain processes, using a dial to emphasize symptom dimensions over dichotomies. These materials use visually engaging metaphor-based illustrations to translate abstract neural processes into intuitive, self-relevant representations emphasizing actionable brain-based learning over brain region labeling. This approach reflects a scalable framework for integrating neuroscience into psychoeducation with the potential to enhance patient understanding, engagement, and support behavioral change in anxiety disorders.

title: Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE): How brain awareness supports brain recovery.
abstract: Over the past two decades, Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation (NIPE) has gradually evolved and become integrated into various therapy modules for psychiatric and neurological disorders. Although NIPE shares certain features with conventional psychoeducation, it is distinguished by key content and structure-related elements. Its content centers on brain-based explanations of the mechanisms and symptoms underlying psychiatric and neurological disorders, as well as the neural processes associated with treatment response, remission, and recovery. NIPE promotes self-awareness and insight and may contribute to motivation for treatment and treatment adherence. It also informs patients, caregivers, and communities how to play an active role in the prevention, treatment, and recovery process based on this mechanistic understanding. Structurally, NIPE is designed to align with how the brain learns and adapts, improving the learning experience to promote more enduring outcomes. By clarifying the processes and goals of brain recovery, increasing self-awareness and self-efficacy, and supporting adherence to prescribed treatments, NIPE may enhance motivation and retention, and facilitate recovery while reducing shame and stigma. This paper provides an introductory overview of NIPE including its definitions and terminology, the current evidence base, clinical implications, and directions for future development.

title: Structural characterization and immunostimulatory activity comparison of two galactofucans from Undaria pinnatifida Sporophyll.
abstract: Two highly sulfated galactofucans were isolated from the sporophylls of Undaria pinnatifida, and their structures were elucidated by methylation analysis, FTIR and NMR spectral analysis, together with HPLC, HPGPC and LXQ (ESI-MS). Comparison of the two U. pinnatifida sporophyll galactofucans (UPSG1 and UPSG2) revealed that UPSG1 exhibited a lower molecular weight than UPSG2 and that O-acetyl groups were present only in UPSG1. Meanwhile, both UPSG1 and UPSG2 possessed a backbone composed of →3)-⍺-L-Fucp4S-(1→, →3,4)-β-D-Galp-(1→, and →3)-β-D-Galp4S-(1 → residues. Moreover, they both showed immunostimulatory activities. Notably, UPSG1 exhibited stronger immunostimulatory activity than UPSG2, as evidenced by its greater capacity to promote NO production and the secretion of TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β, as well as the expression of the M1 marker CD86 in macrophages. In addition, UPSG1 and UPSG2 upregulated the expression of NF-κB, NLRP3, and Caspase-1 proteins, which are involved in inflammatory signaling. The present study elucidates the structure and immunomodulatory activity of U. pinnatifida sporophylls galactofucans, thereby providing a theoretical basis for the utilization of sporophylls, a processing by-product of U. pinnatifida.

title: Assessing apoptotic sensitivity by BH3 profiling in primary mouse B cells.
abstract: Apoptosis and the clearance of dying cells are essential for organismal homeostasis. Excessive cell death contributes to neurodegeneration and autoimmunity, whereas insufficient apoptosis leads to uncontrolled proliferation and cancer. Mitochondria play a key role in the initiation and orchestration of apoptosis through mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation (MOMP). In response to cellular stress, BAX and BAK oligomerise to form pores on the mitochondrial outer membrane, forming conduits through which intermembrane space proteins such as cytochrome c enter the cytoplasm. There, cytochrome c binds APAF1 to form the apoptosome, which recruits and activates caspase-9, triggering downstream activation of caspases-3 and -7, resulting in cell death. MOMP is tightly regulated by the BCL-2 family of proteins, comprising pro-apoptotic effectors (BAX, BAK), pro-apoptotic BH3-only proteins (BID, BIM, PUMA) or anti-apoptotic members (BCL-2, BCL-xL, MCL1). In general, the activity of the pro-apoptotic members is counteracted by the expression of the anti-apoptotic members. However, disruption of this balance leads to induction or sensitisation towards MOMP, and therefore apoptosis. B cell development is governed by a fine balance between survival and apoptotic cell death. Genetic alterations in B cells often lead to overexpression of anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family members, tilting this balance towards survival and enabling defective or malignant B cells to evade cell death. To investigate how mitochondrial apoptotic priming shapes B cell development, we present a protocol for isolating primary mouse B cells that can be readily adapted to diverse disease, including B cell lymphomas. We also describe a BH3 profiling workflow, a robust, accessible assay that assesses mitochondrial apoptotic priming by exposing permeabilised cells to BH3 peptides or small molecule BH3 mimetics and quantifying MOMP by flow cytometric detection of cytochrome c release.
keywords: BH3 Interacting Domain Death Agonist Protein

title: Formal Coercive and Restrictive Measures and Associated Individual Characteristics in Adults With Intellectual Disabilities.
journal: Journal of intellectual disability research : JIDR
abstract: Coercive and restrictive measures used in Norwegian municipal services for adults with intellectual disabilities are regulated and authorised. We evaluated the types, distribution, intensity and differences in individual characteristics across categories of such measures. Adults with intellectual disabilities subject to planned and formally approved coercive and restrictive measures were enrolled. Data were obtained from structured interviews and questionnaires completed primarily by proxy informants, hospital records and municipal decisions regarding such measures. Of 128 eligible individuals, 83 (65%) were included (mean age, 43 years; 75% had severe or profound intellectual disability). The majority lived in group homes with support. The median number of measures per participant was two (range 1-9). Monitoring and alarm systems (60%) and food/drink restrictions (37%) were the most common measures, whereas self-care restrictions were reported in only 12%. For comparative analyses, participants were hierarchically assigned into four mutually exclusive categories based on the most intensive measure: physical/mechanical restraint (n = 28), food/drink/belongings restrictions (n = 33), monitoring and alarm systems (n = 16) and other measures (n = 6). Participants in the physical/mechanical restraint category had the highest informant-rated intensity measure (p < 0.001), the highest number of measures per participant (median = 3) and higher prevalence of autism (43% vs. 16%, p = 0.037) and irritability levels. Participants in the food/drink/belongings restriction category had higher body mass index (median = 28) and better motor function. Coercive and restrictive measures are frequently used in municipal services, with monitoring systems and restrictions predominating. Differences in individual characteristics across defined measure groups highlight the importance of addressing lifestyle-related factors alongside prevention of challenging behaviour.

title: Longitudinal Correlation of Vestibular Function With Symptom Improvements in Vestibular Migraine: A Multicenter Prospective Study.
abstract: To investigate the association between longitudinal changes in vestibular function test (VFT) findings and changes in headache and dizziness symptoms in patients with vestibular migraine (VM). A prospective multicenter study enrolled 126 patients with VM (mean age 40.0± 12.0 years, women=111) from eight referral-base university hospitals in South Korea between February 2022 and May 2024. Patients received preventive treatments for 3 months. Headache and dizziness were assessed at baseline and during the follow-up using structured questionnaires. The VFT included video-oculography (VOG), cervical and ocular vestibular evoked myogenic potentials (VEMPs), and video-head impulse tests (vHIT), which were performed at baseline and follow-up evaluation was arranged for those with abnormal results at baseline. At baseline, VFT findings were abnormal in 54.0% (68/126) of patients with VM: 61.8% on VOG, 60.3% on VEMPs, and 7.4% on vHIT. After 3 months of treatment, the frequency and intensity of dizziness and headache decreased significantly. Among patients with abnormal baseline VFT findings, those whose VFT findings improved showed greater reductions than those with persistent abnormalities in headache intensity (between-group difference, 1.3 points; p=0.036; d=0.52) and dizziness-related quality of life (University of California Los Angeles Dizziness Questionnaire [UCLA-DQ], 2.6 points; p=0.031; d=0.53). Normalization of VOG was associated with greater improvement in headache intensity (1.7 points; p=0.027; d=0.71), whereas normalization of VEMPs was associated with greater improvement in dizziness-related quality of life (UCLA-DQ, 3.3 points; p=0.013; d=0.76). Overall, improvement in VFT abnormalities was associated with improvement in both headache- and dizziness-related measures. Improvements in vestibular function are associated with a reduction in both dizziness and headache in VM, although the observational design precludes causal inference. These findings are consistent with an overlap of vestibular and headache-related networks in the pathophysiology of VM.

title: A Male-Specific Immunometabolic Peripheral Blood Mononuclear Cell Transcriptomic Signature in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) demonstrates well-recognized sex-related differences in incidence, age at onset, and clinical features, but the biological mechanisms underlying this heterogeneity remain incompletely understood. Peripheral immune mechanisms have been proposed as potential contributors. We performed sex-stratified transcriptomic profiling of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) obtained from a clinically well-characterized cohort of 60 participants: 15 male ALS participants, 15 female ALS participants, and 30 sex-matched healthy controls. Differential gene expression and pathway enrichment were analyzed, followed by quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) validation and correlation with clinical parameters, including plasma neurofilament light chain (NfL) levels. PBMCs from male ALS participants exhibited extensive transcriptional alterations, with coordinated downregulation of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation pathways and upregulation of the extracellular matrix and inflammatory signaling. In contrast, PBMCs from female ALS participants showed minimal and less-consistent transcriptomic changes. These findings were validated by qPCR. Notably, changes in mitochondrial and immune-related transcripts were not associated with the plasma NfL level, disease progression rate, or clinical severity. This study has identified a male-specific peripheral immunometabolic transcriptomic signature in ALS that is independent of established biomarkers of neurodegeneration. These findings may help to explain sex-related differences in disease pathogenesis and clinical presentation, and they underscore the importance of considering sex as an influential biological variable in ALS.

title: An open agentic AI co-scientist for clinical and biomedical discovery.
abstract: Biomedical research is constrained by the time and domain expertise required to analyze increasingly large and complex datasets. Here we present OpenScientist, an open-source agentic AI co-scientist designed to address this gap by investigating scientist-defined queries and generating verifiable, data-grounded analyses. OpenScientist was evaluated by domain experts across five biomedical case studies, completing analyses in minutes that otherwise would take months of human time and expertise. It accurately quantified Alzheimer's blood biomarker performance, generated a plasma proteomic survival model that predicted survival in a hidden-evaluation cohort, proposed a reproducible mechanism linking tau pathology to altered lysosomal acidification, generated multiple myeloma hypotheses validated in an external cohort with attenuated signal in randomized controls, and demonstrated concordance with an independent human analysis in a blinded, prespecified proteomic comparison. These results support the use of OpenScientist to assist biomedical data analysis in concert with human experts. To support research involving sensitive clinical datasets, OpenScientist can operate in a fully air-gapped environment using open-source models for inference. OpenScientist demonstrates that open, auditable, agentic AI can support real-world clinical research by researching the literature, generating hypotheses, executing analyses, and generating insights from complex datasets.

title: Peptides and Obesity: Evaluating Intranasal Administration of Peptides for Therapeutic Potential.
journal: Obesity reviews : an official journal of the International Association for the Study of Obesity
abstract: Obesity is a complex global health issue characterized by an imbalance in energy homeostasis and associated with significant health risks, including cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, and cancer. While various therapeutic approaches exist, peptide-based treatments have emerged as promising candidates due to their specificity and reduced side effects. Because many of the mechanisms are centrally regulated in the brain, effective intervention requires peptides with good brain penetration or alternative delivery strategies. In this context, this review explores the potential of intranasal delivery of therapeutic peptide candidates for obesity management, highlighting its advantages in bypassing the blood-brain barrier, targeting central pathways regulating appetite and energy expenditure, and minimizing systemic exposure, while also considering the translational limitations of this delivery route. The review analyses established and emerging peptides, including leptin, GLP-1 analogs, and oxytocin, focusing on their central mechanisms of action, specifically their ability to target the brain. It highlights how these peptides regulate energy homeostasis, appetite, and metabolism through direct activation of neural circuits in the hypothalamus, brainstem, and other key regions involved in obesity management. Furthermore, it evaluates the prospects of intranasal peptide therapeutics as an innovative strategy in obesity treatment, addressing both the opportunities and limitations in the context of clinical and preclinical evidence. Continued research and technological advancements are essential to optimize peptide formulations and delivery systems, ensuring efficacy, safety, and patient compliance in combating the obesity epidemic.

title: Distinct patterns of activity in the prelimbic cortex track task-related differences for cocaine and water reinforcers.
abstract: The pursuit of drugs is a fundamental element of substance use. Different tasks assess drug pursuit in the face of effort, punishment, or the absence of the drug, and recent studies have suggested that a shared latent variable may drive behavior across these tasks. The prelimbic cortex (PL) is implicated in these behaviors, but it is unknown if its role is driven by distinct neural ensembles. We recorded PL activity using in vivo endoscopic calcium imaging in 32 male and female Sprague-Dawley rats as they completed cocaine or water self-administration, extinction, progressive ratio, and punished self-administration. We found that behavior across tasks covaried in water, but not cocaine rats. We also found that slow, sustained neural excitations following response for reward were lower in extinction. Furthermore, exploratory analysis suggests that those individual rats that had more responsive neurons also had significantly higher levels of reward pursuit in the extinction task. Notably, this relationship was true across cocaine and water rats, suggesting a general role independent of reward type. Thus, our findings suggest that extinction behavior is tracked by a distinct neural pattern in the PL.

title: Nature, Nurture, and Early Childhood Development: Emerging Evidence and Opportunities for Pediatrics.
abstract: Early childhood represents a unique window of biological vulnerability and developmental opportunity1. Brain plasticity during the first years of life suggests that environmental exposures and relational experiences may exert profound and lasting effects on cognitive, emotional, and physical health throughout the lifespan2,3. Within the framework of contemporary developmental neuroscience, pediatric research has increasingly focused on how physical surroundings, particularly green spaces and natural environments, interact with socio-emotional experiences to shape early developmental trajectories. A major research initiative recently announced in Europe, by the Royal Foundation Centre for Early Childhood4, brings this intersection to the forefront. This commentary authored by members of the working group on Social Pediatrics of the European Pediatric Association, Union of National Pediatric Societies and Associations (EPA-UNEPSA), briefly explores current evidence across environmental psychology and pediatric developmental research, reporting recent parental survey data, with the aim to highlight the opportunities and methodological challenges this initiative may present for social and preventive pediatrics.

title: Comparing the acute neurophysiological effects of 10 Hz monophasic cTMS and biphasic rTMS in healthy adults.
abstract: Neurophysiological responses to repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) are highly variable across individuals. Monophasic stimulation using controllable pulse parameter TMS (cTMS) has been shown to enhance corticospinal excitability and increase responder rates in patterned protocols. However, it remains unclear whether these advantages extend to conventional 10 Hz stimulation. To compare the acute effects of 10 Hz monophasic cTMS and biphasic rTMS on corticospinal excitability and short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI), and to examine the influence of sex and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) genotype. Thirty-three healthy adults completed three randomized sessions of 10 Hz cTMS, rTMS, and sham stimulation. Motor evoked potentials (MEPs) and SICI were assessed at baseline and 10 min post-stimulation. Responders were classified based on changes in MEP amplitude. No significant changes in MEP amplitude or SICI were observed following cTMS, rTMS, or sham. Exploratory analysis detected no significant effects of sex or BDNF genotype. Exploratory responder analyses revealed substantial variability, with similar proportions of facilitation following cTMS (61%) and rTMS (64%). Across real stimulation, facilitation was observed in 57% of Val/Val and 68% of Met carriers, with no clear differences between genotypes. No significant differences were detected between 10 Hz monophasic cTMS, biphasic rTMS, and sham in MEP amplitude or SICI at 10 min post-stimulation. Exploratory analyses detected no clear effects of sex or BDNF genotype.

title: Beta1-adrenergic receptor regulation of VMN growth hormone-releasing hormone neuron lactate, estrogen, and counterregulatory transmitter receptor gene expression in male versus female rats.
abstract: The metabolic-sensitive hindbrain transmitter norepinephrine (NE) controls ventromedial hypothalamic nucleus (VMN) growth hormone-releasing hormone (Ghrh)/steroidogenic factor-1 (SF1) neuron counterregulatory neurotransmission via beta1-adrenergic receptor signaling. Ghrh neurons assimilate nutrient, hormone, and neurochemical cues that affect counterregulation. Current research employed in vivo ADRβ1 gene silencing technology to examine whether NE imposes sex-specific regulation of VMN Ghrh neuron receptivity to these stimuli during eu- and/or hypoglycemia. VMN ADRβ1 gene knockdown respectively up- or down-regulated Ghrh neuron GPR81 lactate receptor gene expression in vehicle- versus insulin-injected male rats, yet this mRNA was decreased (euglycemia) or unaffected (hypoglycemia) in females. Gene silencing suppressed estrogen receptor (ER)-alpha, ER-beta, and G protein-coupled ER-1 (GPER) transcripts in euglycemic females but negatively only a subset of these mRNAs in males. β1-AR knockdown did not modify ER gene expression in insulin-treated female rats but inhibited GPER transcripts in hypoglycemic males. Eu- and hypoglycemic animals of each sex exhibited down-regulated Ghrh neuron gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-A receptor mRNA after VMN ADRβ1 siRNA pretreatment, whereas gene silencing correspondingly decreased or increased GABA-B receptor subunit-2 transcripts in hypoglycemic males versus females. ADRβ1 gene knockdown caused opposite changes in guanylate cyclase-1 soluble subunit alpha2 mRNA in vehicle- versus insulin-treated males but down-regulated this mRNA in females. Results suggest that sex-dimorphic β1-AR control of VMNdm Ghrh/SF-1 neuron transmission may involve regulation of cell sensitivity to convergent extrinsic stimuli that influence neural regulation of glucose homeostasis. Data moreover disclose that the direction of receptor control of distinctive receptor genes is glucose status-dependent.

title: Acupuncture alleviates post-stroke depression by inhibiting proline-driven ferroptosis in hippocampal neurons.
abstract: Post-stroke depression (PSD) represents a prevalent stroke complication with scarce therapeutic interventions. Acupuncture has shown clinical efficacy in PSD, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigates whether acupuncture alleviates PSD by regulating proline metabolism-mediated ferroptosis. We generated a rat PSD model via common carotid artery ligation coupled with chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS). Acupuncture at GV20, GV26, GV24, and GV14 was administered for four weeks. Behavioral tests, TTC and Nissl staining, ELISA, qPCR, western blot, amino acid metabolomics, and hippocampal neuron cultures with proline intervention were performed. Acupuncture robustly rescued depression-like phenotypes and mitigated hippocampal neuronal injury in PSD rats. Acupuncture decreased serum levels of iron ions, malondialdehyde (MDA) and reactive oxygen species (ROS), increased glutathione (GSH), and reversed the aberrant expression of ferroptosis-related proteins (GPX4, SLC7A11, ACSL4, TFR1) in the hippocampus. Amino acid metabolomics revealed elevated serum proline in PSD rats, which was normalized by acupuncture. Exogenous proline administration aggravated depressive behaviors and hippocampal ferroptosis. In cultured hippocampal neurons, high-dose proline directly induced ferroptosis and reduced cell viability. Acupuncture ameliorates PSD by inhibiting hippocampal neuronal ferroptosis through regulation of proline metabolism, revealing a novel mechanism for acupuncture treatment.

title: Isoform-specific conformational dynamics in proteasome activator 28 kDa define alternative allosteric regulation of the human 20S proteasome.
abstract: The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) preserves proteome integrity, and its dysfunction is linked to neurodegenerative diseases of the brain and retina. The human 20S proteasome (h20S) is activated by the Proteasome Activator 28 kDa (PA28) isoforms PA28αβ and PA28γ, yet the molecular basis of their differential interactions remains incompletely understood. Here, biochemical assays, kinetic and thermodynamic modelling, surface plasmon resonance and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations reveal distinct isoform-specific mechanisms. PA28αβ binds h20S with higher affinity and model-derived positive cooperativity (K = 5.0 × 1010 M-1; δ = 2.5), exhibiting single-exponential binding kinetics and broader conformational sampling in its unbound state. By contrast, PA28γ displays lower affinity, model-derived negative cooperativity (K = 1.25 × 109 M-1; δ = 0.15), where a biphasic binding process refers to an initial intermediate followed by a subsequent stabilization, potentially associated with an induced-fit-like rearrangement. This behavior is accompanied by more restricted conformational sampling of unbound PA28γ. These findings provide new insights into the molecular basis of PA28 isoform-specific h20S regulation and link proteasome dynamics to proteostasis-driven disease.

title: Editorial: Impact of nutrition on brain health.
Differential associations of contralesional and ipsilesional brain functional connectivity with lower-limb impairment after stroke.
abstract: Stroke may induce distinct plastic structural changes within the ipsilesional and contralesional hemispheres of the brain, leading to interhemispheric imbalances in cortical connectivity. Maximum joint range of motion (ROMmax) impairments may also occur in the paretic limb, contributing to increased interlimb asymmetry and impaired gait. This study examined the influence of ipsilesional and contralesional brain functional connectivity on hip flexion ROMmax interlimb asymmetry and walking performance in stroke survivors. Eighteen individuals with chronic stroke (57.5 ± 14.8 years; 26.7 ± 22.2 months post-stroke) were assessed for functional connectivity of the ipsilesional and contralesional general hemispheres and specific primary motor cortex (M1) areas of the brain with resting-state electroencephalography (EEG). Participants were also assessed for hip flexion active ROMmax of the paretic and non-paretic limbs and 10-m walk test, and ROMmax interlimb asymmetry was further calculated. Relationships between changes in these variables were examined by Pearson product-moment (r) and regression analyses. Hip flexion ROMmax interlimb asymmetry was significantly associated with contralesional functional connectivity in both general (r = 0.53) and M1-specific (r = 0.48) regions of the brain (P < 0.05). Walking performance was only associated with contralesional M1 connectivity (r = 0.51; P < 0.05). Contralesional hemisphere connectivity explained 28% of the variance in ROMmax asymmetry, while contralesional M1 connectivity explained 26% of the variance in walking time. No significant relationships were found for brain connectivity within the ipsilesional hemisphere. Greater brain functional connectivity in contralesional cortical regions is associated with increased hip ROMmax asymmetry and impaired walking performance in stroke survivors, highlighting the role of contralesional networks in post-stroke motor impairment.

title: Effects of Intravenous Dexamethasone on IL-6 Levels in Children Undergoing Cardiac Surgery With Cardiopulmonary Bypass.
abstract: Cardiopulmonary bypass provokes a systemic inflammatory response in children, with interleukin-6 (IL-6) levels rising rapidly after bypass. Corticosteroids are frequently used to blunt this response, but paediatric evidence remains inconsistent. To evaluate whether a single intravenous dose of dexamethasone reduces the post-bypass increase in plasma IL-6 and improves early postoperative outcomes in children undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass. This single-centre quasi-experimental study enrolled 46 children aged one month to 12 years undergoing elective repair of congenital heart disease between January 2025 and August 2025. Participants were purposively recruited and alternately allocated to intravenous dexamethasone (1 mg/kg, maximum 10 mg; n=23, 50.0%) or 2 mL normal saline (n=23, 50.0%) after induction of anaesthesia. Plasma IL-6 was measured before drug administration, two hours after cardiopulmonary bypass, and 24 hours after bypass. Haemodynamic variables, oxygen saturation, extubation time, and intensive care unit stay were recorded. The median IL-6 increase from baseline to two hours was lower with dexamethasone than with saline (261.90 pg/mL, interquartile range: 195.0-824.0, versus 447.0 pg/mL, interquartile range: 261.70-1,230.20), but the difference was not statistically significant (p=0.177). At 24 hours, the median change from baseline was 8.20 pg/mL in the dexamethasone group and 13.0 pg/mL in the saline group (p=0.350). Blood pressure, oxygen saturation, and extubation time were comparable. First-postoperative-day heart rate was higher with dexamethasone (143.63 ± 18.93 versus 117.76 ± 19.57 beats/min; p=0.001), and median intensive care unit stay was longer (120 versus 95.5 hours; p=0.001).
