Among 128 individuals analysed, patients with B-CLPD showed significant immunological and clinical differences compared to healthy controls, particularly in vaccine-specific antibody responses and lymphocyte subsets. B-CLPD patients with recurrent or severe infections exhibited markedly reduced pre-vaccination anti-pneumococcal (p = 0.03) and post-vaccination anti-pneumococcal (p = 0.001) and anti-Salmonella typhi Vi titers (p = 0.1), highlighting impaired vaccine-specific antibody responses as potential predictors of infection risk. An immunological classification identified two subgroups within B-CLPD, predominant antibody defect and combined immune defect, with a trend toward higher respiratory infection rates in the latter, suggesting broader immune dysfunction.

title: Extracellular vesicles and their role in neurodegenerative diseases.
abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are membrane-bound nanoparticles that enable intercellular communication in the nervous system by transferring proteins, lipids and nucleic acids between cells. In neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs), evidence from cellular and animal models, together with emerging human data, implicates EVs in several interconnected processes: altered vesicle biogenesis and endolysosomal trafficking; selective loading of pathogenic cargoes (including amyloid-β, tau, α-synuclein, TDP43 and PrPSc); and dissemination of misfolded proteins in ways consistent with prion-like seeding and spread. EVs also modulate neuroinflammation by relaying cytokines and regulatory microRNAs among neurons, glia and the neurovascular unit and by engaging the blood-brain barrier to shape CNS-periphery crosstalk. These same properties underpin a growing translational interest: brain-derived EV populations in blood and other biofluids offer a minimally invasive window into early pathology and disease trajectories, and native or engineered EVs are being developed as delivery vehicles or as targets to curb pathological propagation. This Review integrates mechanistic and clinical advances, highlights key sources of biological and methodological variability, and defines priorities for standardization, cell-of-origin assignment and clinical validation required to realize EV-based diagnostics and therapeutics for NDDs.

title: Chronic boat noise exposure elevates boldness and anxiety-like behaviour, while impairing learning in juvenile cichlids Maylandia zebra.
abstract: Underwater anthropogenic noise is a pervasive environmental stressor, yet its impact on the ontogeny of cognitive processes and behavioural coping styles in fish remains poorly understood. This study investigates how chronic exposure to boat noise during early development affects the behavioural phenotype and associative learning in juvenile cichlids (Maylandia zebra). Using a split-brood design to control for genetic variation, siblings were reared under either control (lab-silent) or intermittent boat noise conditions for 12 weeks. Subjects were subsequently tested to assess boldness, anxiety-like responses, social aggression, and aversive learning performance. Results revealed that chronic noise exposure induced a complex shift in coping behaviours: noise-reared juveniles exhibited faster engagement with novel objects (indicating increased risk-taking) but simultaneously displayed heightened anxiety-like responses in light/dark preference tests, compared to the silent-reared control group. Noise-reared fish also showed impaired performance on a colour discrimination learning task conducted under silent conditions. These findings demonstrate that the cognitive deficit was not a result of acute attentional distraction, but rather a persistent consequence of developmental stress. Conversely, social aggression was unaffected by rearing history and decreased only during acute noise playback. These findings suggest that early-life acoustic stress reshapes the behavioural phenotype towards a high-anxiety, reactive state and imposes lasting costs on cognitive integrity, potentially compromising fitness in noise-polluted ecosystems.

title: Adolescent social isolation and re-socialization increases alcohol intake and aversion-resistant drinking in male and female rats.
abstract: Adverse experiences during adolescence, especially social isolation, increases risk for alcohol use disorders (AUDs). Previous rodent studies of adolescent social isolation (ASI) encompassed all stages of adolescence and/or maintained isolation into adulthood, limiting identification of vulnerable stages of adolescence. Utilizing males only, or combining the sexes, also may have contributed to contradictory findings. Investigate social isolation restricted to discrete adolescent stages in combination with re-socialization and then persistent alcohol drinking. Determine whether adolescent isolation during specific developmental time periods, with or without subsequent re-socialization, leads to increased alcohol drinking in males or females. Male and female Wistar rats underwent one of six housing conditions: (1) isolation from postnatal day (P)21-42 followed by re-socialization (ASIR-Early), (2) isolation from P42-63 followed by re-socialization (ASIR-Late), or (3) continuous isolation from P21 onward (ASI), or (4​-6) one of three appropriate control treatments. Alcohol-related behaviors were assessed in adulthood using intermittent-access two-bottle choice drinking (IAP), limited daily access (LDA-20) procedures, quinine-adulterated aversion-resistant drinking (ARD), and alcohol re-exposure following prolonged abstinence. In general, ASIR-Early and ASI elevated alcohol drinking in males and females, when compared to contemporary controls, during IAP, LDA-20, ARD, and after prolonged withdrawal, while ASIR-Late had largely similar effects as control conditions. However, for females, only ASI led to greater ARD at the highest quinine dose and also increased alcohol drinking after prolonged withdrawal. In contrast, for males, ASIR-Early and ASI had largely similar enhancement of alcohol drinking. Under these conditions, isolation housing that encompassed the early adolescent period produced enduring increases in alcohol-related behaviors, with re-socialization perhaps more protective in females against ARD and elevated intake after abstinence. These results inform future studies that will investigate neural mechanisms underlying ASI-induced enhancement of alcohol drinking.

title: Causal role of human hippocampus in relational structure learning and inference.
abstract: When meeting new individuals or known individuals in new circumstances, we intuitively map out their relationships-not merely through direct experience, but by inferring new connections on the basis of prior relational knowledge. How such relational knowledge is represented and used in the brain remains a long-standing question in cognitive neuroscience. Here, using a behavioural task and computational modelling, we show that participants (N = 36) leveraged existing knowledge of relational structures to infer new relationships, facilitating adaptation in changing environments. Whole-brain neuroimaging identified consistent representations of relational structure in the hippocampus. To investigate the causal link between hippocampal representations and inference, we used neural network simulations to predict the behavioural effects of disrupting such representations. Consistent with this prediction, transcranial ultrasound stimulation of the human hippocampus (N = 20), transiently modulating its activity, disrupted structure-based inference (P < 0.001, Cohen's d = -0.89, 95% confidence interval -1.41 to -0.36), providing empirical evidence for a causal role of hippocampus in relational-structure learning and structure-based inference.
